newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Abducted Briton's fate in Cambodia still a mystery.
newsitem.headline: Abducted Briton's fate in Cambodia still a mystery.

text.p: The fate of British mine clearance supervisor Christopher Howes is still a mystery one year after he was abducted by gunmen in northern Cambodia.
Military officials say they are not sure whether he is alive.
Hope has not been given up for Howes and his interpreter, Houn Hourth, who were believed abducted by hardline Khmer Rouge guerrillas on March 26 last year.
Howes, 37, from Bristol, and his aide are believed to have been taken to the northwestern Khmer Rouge base of Anlong Veng after their abduction in the province of Siem Reap.
However a new hostage crisis has pushed the fate of Howes and Hourth, employees of the British-based Mines Advisory Group (MAG), into the backgrond.

A team of 15 Cambodian officials and pilots flew into rebel territory on February 24 to try to persuade the one-legged Khmer Rouge commander, Ta Mok, to defect with his guerrillas, but they have been held ever since.

"The English de-miner is now a small thing, the main thing is the 15 officials and the helicopter and national reconciliation," Major-General Khan Savoeun, the officer in charge of the search for Howes, recently told Reuters.
Military officials have said they believe Howes and Hourth, who were abducted not far from the 12th century Angkor Wat and other temples popular with tourists, were taken to Anlong Veng.
But there has never been confirmation, while the Khmer Rouge have denied holding Howes.
"If we reach the real national reconciliation in Anlong Veng, everyone will come out including the English mine-clearer," said Khan Savoeun.

His deputy, General Long Sareirath, told Reuters: "We are only concentrating on getting the Khmer Rouge hardliners in Anlong Veng to join the government and we are not sure if the Englishman is still alive."

He and most others, including the British government, are pinning their hopes on a settlement being reached with the guerrillas in Anlong Veng, and Howes and Hourth being discovered alive in the rebel base.

The Maoist-inspired Khmer Rouge, whose 1975-79 "killing fields" rule left more than a million people dead, began falling apart after the two men were abducted, with thousands of guerrillas joining the Cambodian government in the past seven months.
Hopes were raised last November when armed forces deputy chief of staff General Nhiek Bun Chhay said the two MAG employees had escaped and were heading towards government lines.
They never showed up, dealing another blow to hopes raised for his parents, Roy and Betty Howes, who have had a frustrating and harrowing year as a result of the many conflicting reports.

A British source said they were "incandescent with rage" on discovering that a guerrilla jailed for his part in the abduction had been released. They wrote letters of complaint to Cambodian co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen.

"Until we have confirmation that Chris and Houn are no longer alive, which probably means seeing their bodies, we will assume they are still alive and we will go on making every possible effort to get their release," said MAG programme director Ian Brown, reflecting the British government stand.
Others are pessimistic, noting the record of the Khmer Rouge, who reneged on a 1991 U.N.-brokered peace pact and have fought the coalition government formed in 1993.
The group has kidnapped more than a dozen Westerners since the coalition was formed and killed at least seven of them.
